title: Contemplate and share
hook: the friars' life: prayer and study fill the basin, and preaching is what spills over

segments.voice: Yesterday, veritas: truth as someone to follow, and truth told in charity. Your line was veritas. Did the true sentence get said, and how did it land? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-four.

Two ways to move water. A channel takes in water at one end and lets it out the other, at the same moment. Always flowing, never full. A basin fills first. It takes the water in, holds it, and only when it's full to the brim does it spill over the edge, and it stays full while it spills. Bernard of Clairvaux, a Cistercian monk, used this picture in a sermon. Too many people, he said, are channels, and he wished they were basins. Later, a Dominican friar put the same idea into a short Latin phrase, and his order took it up as a motto. Today: fill first, then spill.
screen: `A CHANNEL: ALWAYS FLOWING, NEVER FULL.` → `A BASIN: FILLS FIRST, THEN SPILLS.` → `BERNARD WISHED FOR BASINS.`

segments.voice: The friar was Thomas Aquinas. In his Summa, he asks a practical question: what kind of religious life is best? A life of pure prayer, hidden away? A life of pure action, out in the streets? His answer is neither by itself. The best, he says, is to contemplate, and to hand on to others what you have contemplated. In Latin, contemplari et contemplata aliis tradere. His reason is a lovely image. It is a greater thing, he writes, to give light than only to shine. A lamp that glows in a closed room is good. A lamp carried into a dark street is better. That is the Dominican shape of life. The friars pray the hours together in choir. They study. And then they go out and preach. The preaching isn't meant to be a performance or a sales pitch. It's meant to be overflow, the basin spilling over. Jesus says something close to this in Matthew's Gospel. In the Douay-Rheims: "out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh." Whatever fills you is what comes out. Notice the order of the words, though. Contemplate first. Then share. A friar who only talks runs dry; a friar who only prays keeps the light in the closet. The phrase also works as a small test. Before you give advice, have you looked long at the thing? And after you've looked long, did anyone else get to see it?
screen: `AQUINAS: WHICH LIFE IS BEST?` · `CONTEMPLATE, THEN HAND IT ON.` · `BETTER TO GIVE LIGHT THAN ONLY SHINE.` · `PRAY, STUDY, THEN PREACH.` · then, large: `OUT OF THE ABUNDANCE OF THE HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: share one fruit of prayer. Settle, and breathe. Look back over this week's quiet moments: a line from a psalm, a thought on a walk, something that struck you during one of these sits. Let one of them come forward. Don't pick the most impressive one. Pick the one that still feels warm. Hold it for a few breaths. Now bring to mind one person who might need exactly that. A friend who's tired. A parent who worries. If you pray, you can give thanks for what you received, and ask for the right moment to pass it on. If not, simply hold the thought and the person side by side. The bell holds the time.
Contemplate and share. Look long at God, then hand on what you've seen: a Dominican motto, from Thomas Aquinas. Today's word.
Your line: overflow. Today, pass the warm thought to the person you pictured, in a sentence or a message. Let it be spillover, not a speech. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-four.

original.note: Latin, from Thomas Aquinas: to hand on to others the things contemplated. a Dominican motto.

what it means: looking long at God, then handing on what you saw. prayer fills the basin; preaching is the spill.
